subject: Canada's jobless rate hit 6.7% nine days after a hike
bodyMarkdown:
Canada's October jobs numbers landed yesterday morning, and they say something quite different from what the Bank of Canada said nine days earlier. If you are looking for work, or you have a mortgage renewing inside the next year, that gap is what I would watch between now and December 9.

## The flat headline hid a split

Employment fell by 4,700 in October and the unemployment rate rose to 6.7 per cent from 6.5, a six-month high, CBC reported on Friday. Forecasts had been for a gain of about 13,600, so the print came in roughly 18,000 jobs below what the street expected, and it was the third monthly decline in a row. Underneath that flat headline, private sector employees fell by about 53,000, the first drop since February, while public sector employment rose by roughly 50,000 after four straight monthly declines. Those two numbers are not the same kind of news. Wholesale and retail trade shed 29,000 positions, Retail Insider reported on Friday, and the sector is down 113,000 over twelve months. Construction added 16,000. Youth unemployment climbed 0.7 points to 13.7 per cent.

## The Bank hiked into this

On October 28 the Bank of Canada raised its **overnight rate**, the rate banks charge each other for one-night loans and the anchor under prime and variable mortgages, by a quarter point to 2.50 per cent. First increase since July 2023, after seven holds at 2.25. The reason Tiff Macklem gave was energy: CPI inflation ran above 3 per cent in September, past the top of the Bank's 1 to 3 per cent target range, with energy doing most of the work, and he wanted to stop it from becoming general. Nine days later the labour market handed him the counterargument. Pricing in the swaps market for a December 9 hike slipped after the release, to roughly 32 per cent from 40 on one reading. TD Securities' Emma Lawrence was unmoved, saying the report "is likely not enough to strongly weaken the case for a December hike."

## The loonie paid for the divergence

Here is the part I find uncomfortable. The same morning, the United States reported 165,000 new payroll jobs in October against forecasts near 65,000, with unemployment down to 4.1 per cent, and market odds on a Fed hike at the December 8 and 9 meeting jumped to somewhere near 78 per cent (estimates vary by source). The Fed is holding at 3.75 to 4.00 per cent. Two central banks are being pushed the same way by economies that look nothing alike, one running hot and one absorbing an oil shock. The Canadian dollar fell about 0.7 per cent to 1.4110 per US dollar, its weakest since October 19, and the Globe and Mail reported on Friday that it was heading for its worst week since late September. A cheaper loonie makes imported goods dearer, which is the inflation the Bank says it is fighting.

## The takeaway

October CPI lands in mid-November, and that is the number that settles December 9, not this jobs report. I would not plan around cuts; the honest range is a hold or one more quarter point, and CIBC's Andrew Grantham has said he does not think the policy rate needs to go above 2.75 per cent. If you are job hunting, the hiring right now is in construction and public payrolls while retail keeps shrinking. If you are a student, 13.7 per cent youth unemployment means starting applications earlier than feels necessary.
